titre: The Lockheed Scandal Invents the Crime of Bribing Abroad
accroche: In 1976, a bribe paid to a former Japanese prime minister pushes the United States to invent, a year later, the world's first crime of foreign bribery.
contenu_vulgarise:
In July 1976, Japanese police arrest former Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka. The charge is not an ordinary abuse of power: he allegedly took about three million dollars to favor the purchase, by a Japanese airline, of aircraft built by the American company Lockheed. Yet the affair did not break in Japan. It comes from the documents of a U.S. Senate committee.

## A Slush Fund Found by Accident

The investigation was not originally aimed at bribery abroad. After Watergate, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is tracking the slush funds that American companies have used to secretly finance election campaigns. Combing through Lockheed's books, it discovers something else: $22 million paid, from the late 1950s to the mid-1970s, to officials and intermediaries in Japan, the Netherlands, Italy, and elsewhere, to win aircraft contracts.

The Senate subcommittee on multinational corporations, chaired by Frank Church, hears from Gulf Oil, Northrop, and Mobil Oil over the course of 1975, then from Lockheed's executives, whose testimony on February 6, 1976, is the most striking. Church announces it at the opening of the hearings: this is not, he says, a question of private morality. It is a foreign policy problem. What the proceedings reveal goes beyond a single industrial group: the SEC's investigations, which continue until 1977, identify in all more than 400 American companies that made questionable payments to foreign officials or parties, totaling more than $300 million.

## The First Country to Ban It for Itself

On December 19, 1977, President Jimmy Carter signs the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. The law operates on two levels: it prohibits any American company, or any company listed in the United States, from making a payment to a foreign public official to obtain or retain business, and it requires listed companies to keep books accurate enough that a slush fund can no longer hide in them. In his signing statement, published the next day, Carter writes that he shares the belief of Congress: bribery is ethically repugnant and competitively unnecessary.

The shift is here. For the first time, a country commits to punishing its own companies for acts committed outside its territory, against the officials of another state, even if that state would never prosecute them itself. Twenty years later, a 1998 amendment implements an OECD convention that aims to extend a comparable prohibition to the other major exporting economies.

carte.punch: A bribe to a Japanese prime minister pushes the United States to punish its own companies.
carte.idee: In 1976, an investigation opened after Watergate reveals that Lockheed paid $22 million to foreign officials, including former Japanese Prime Minister Tanaka. On December 19, 1977, the United States forbids its companies to bribe a foreign official.

quiz.question: What exactly did the SEC discover when investigating Lockheed's slush funds after Watergate?
choix: That Lockheed had falsified its books to hide commercial losses from its shareholders
That Lockheed was selling military aircraft to countries under an American embargo
That Lockheed was employing foreign nationals without work authorization
That Lockheed had paid $22 million to foreign officials to win contracts
quiz.explication: The investigation, opened for reasons of accounting transparency after Watergate, uncovered payments to foreign officials, not a mere financial irregularity internal to the company.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the SEC investigation that led to the discovery of Lockheed's payments abroad originally aimed at?
choix: Sales of American military aircraft to countries under embargo
The tax fraud of several Japanese aerospace subcontractors
Slush funds used by American companies to secretly finance election campaigns
The covert financing of a Dutch political party by industrial groups
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After Watergate, the SEC was tracking slush funds used to secretly finance election campaigns, and it was while combing through Lockheed's books that it discovered the payments abroad.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which companies had the Senate subcommittee chaired by Frank Church already heard before Lockheed on comparable facts?
choix: Gulf Oil, Northrop, and Mobil Oil
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The subcommittee had already heard from Gulf Oil, Northrop, and Mobil Oil over the course of 1975, before questioning Lockheed's executives, whose testimony came on February 6, 1976.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act signed in 1977 make possible for the first time?
choix: That foreign companies be tried by American courts for any offense committed at home
That the SEC obtain the power to dissolve a company found guilty of bribery
That the U.S. Congress approve each arms export contract case by case
That a country punish its own companies for bribery committed abroad
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text stresses that, for the first time, a country commits to punishing its own companies for acts committed outside its territory, against the officials of another state.
